doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Woody Herman, Chubby Jackson and Europe
title: First trip to Europe and audience reaction
summary: Audiences treated jazz musicians like royalty, with flowers thrown on stage; Gibbs adds remarks on cocky Americans and his long marriage.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: What was your first reaction to Europe like? The first time you went?

It was amazing. I mean the reaction of the audience for the musicians. I didn’t believe it. The first concert we played after we got done, 84,000 flowers were put on stage. I never saw — for a jazz concert? I never saw that. But jazz musicians, especially this was 1946 I think it was or early ’47. The jazz musician was treated like Toscanini, like a symphony musician, got the same feeling you get from the audience, they gave you that feeling of greatness. They appreciate what you did. And you were treated like royalty. It’s a little different now. You know it’s still good, they fill up jazz there you know—
Yeah, but it’s not quite like you’re conquering heroes or—
Well not so much anymore. In a few years of going to Europe, I’ll tell you, the cocky American.

I mean not really, let’s face it, the jazz musicians in America are the best. They are the best. So I think, and also I think some of the countrymen have resented the jazz musicians taking some of their ladies away to the United States, so that wasn’t a good thing either.

Not me. Not me. Thank God. I’ve been married now, this time, for 23 years. And my wife is the greatest thing that ever lived. Anybody who will put up with me for 23 years, you know has got to be a complete — well she’s out of it probably. My wife is saying it don’t make any sense. She doesn’t understand half of the things I say to her. She just comes right out and — that’s why she’s with me.
Well that’s right. Hope she never does.
You know, another 25 years, “I know what he said 20 years ago now.” It’ll come to her.
